So I think the answer to your second part of the question is no, that is really not the case. There was, for example, no suggestion that the other two peoples would receive constituent nation status in the Serbian state. And in fact, never did, and that was never seriously considered until about a year ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, can we agree that the March 1992, the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, proclaimed independence following referendum in February which was organised by Bosnian Muslims, with a certain amount of support from Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, you have asked several questions there. Was there --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me simplify. I would like to know whether in March 1992 there was an Assembly meeting of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was it held without the presence of the representatives of the Serb people on that occasion, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree the representatives of the SDA did not attend the session.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, I am referring to the Assembly of the Bosnia-Herzegovina after the referendum in March 1992.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the representatives of the SDA -- I am sorry, the SDS. If I said "SDA," I spoke incorrectly. The representatives of the SDS, that is deputies in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did not attend that session.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any knowledge about the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina following that referendum proclaiming the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They did so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the referendum was held by the end of February and the beginning of March of that year, 1992, and that it was organised by the Bosnian Muslims with the support of the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, there are two questions there. The referendum was held on the last day of February, which is 29th of February, and the first day of March. It was organised by order of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and with the endorsement or similar act of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, at the suggestion of the Badinter Commission of the European community.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, isn't it correct that the right -- that the decision, sorry, about proclaiming the independence was counter to Articles 1 and 2 of the Constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not a constitutional expert and I am not really prepared or don't feel I am qualified to render that decision or that judgment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Donia. You have told us that the opinion of the Badinter Commission was sought. Have you got any knowledge about the Badinter Commission of the European Community issuing any opinions on the occasion of the referendum and on the occasion of the proclamation of independence? Let me try -- I would like to simplify the question but I am unable to. Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on those two occasions, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And if I tell you that the Badinter Commission did issue an opinion, will you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And if I tell you that the opinion was as follows: "Acting according to the will of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina for the socialist republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina being set up as a sovereign and independent state, not being able to be considered as fully well-founded."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are citing a document, I would like to examine the document. It very well may be that that statement was made by the Badinter Commission but I don't have any first-hand knowledge of it and would like to examine any document that made that statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't have that document at the moment, but I have tried and I did my best to try and quote as best I could the exact wording. Mr. Donia, would you agree that the results of that referendum led to an escalation of nationalist behaviour on the part of the members of nationalist parties on all sides? And I am referring to Sarajevo in particular at the moment.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that these events represent the beginning of the conflict which then degenerated into armed conflict in Sarajevo and the rest of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why you say no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is extremely difficult to identify a single beginning point to the armed conflict. There was armed conflict that began in very early April, April 1. That, to me, is a good starting date but I think there is also good reason to look at April 6th or April 4th as dates that are good starting points for the armed conflict. The events that begin to lead up to it, I think should be dated considerably further back than that, than the date that you have suggested and it is very difficult, I think, to identify a specific point in time which one should say, "This is where it began and nothing previous to this really influenced the development of the conflict." So I have difficulty identifying any date as the beginning of the particular conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said in your expertise, in your export report, that there were barricades in Sarajevo. Can you tell us when exactly the first barricades were erected in Sarajevo? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within a few hours of the completion of the voting, the first barricades went up in the Pofalici area. That was the -- that was the late night, late evening of 1 March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about what happened after the vote in favour of the independence on the occasion of that referendum, of the fact that this victory was celebrated in an improper way in some parts of town and in some parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the part of the SDA party?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know specifically what you are referring to. There was plenty of celebrating. Some of it was probably excessive, but there were also acts of violence that occurred within hours of this event, which I think are not necessarily related to either the referendum itself or the celebrations that took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that the cause of the conflict in the area of the city of Sarajevo, or rather, do you have any knowledge of there having been one person killed on the 1st of March of that year, one Serb person, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I referred to that in my report. If I recall, the --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- father of the groom of a wedding that was taking place, that had taken place in the old Serbian Orthodox church in Sarajevo, was killed just after this had taken place, and the post-wedding celebration was going on in Bascarsija and at that point a shot or shots -- there were several shots fired, killing the father of the groom and wounding an Orthodox priest.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, do you believe that as of that day Sarajevo was a divided city, first of all, the barricades and then there was military and the political division? Do you believe that that was one of the causes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several questions, again. Was Sarajevo a divided city as of that day? No. I think some territorial division was in the process of taking place, but the city was, once the barricades came down, free and open again and really not divided. There was by that time a significant political division, with the SDS having take power in several of the municipalities, as I indicated, around the periphery of the city. The military division of the city was really not yet established. The barricades clearly stopped free movement for a period of about 24 hours to 48 hours, but then it was restored again.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Donia. On page 7 of your paragraph [as interpreted], you refer to military preparations on the part of the nationalist parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You say that all nationalist parties started preparing for war. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On page 7, you said that the SDA set up two paramilitary units, the Patriotic League and the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was in command there, who was the commander of those paramilitary units? Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I couldn't name you -- I don't know the names of the commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when they were set up?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know much about the Green Berets unit. The -- I am aware that the Patriotic League had only a skeleton organisation until September/October of 19 -- or September/October of 1991, when some of the command positions were filled by Muslims who had left the JNA in the wake of events in Croatia, which had made the JNA into an increasingly Serbian force in Croatia. That organisation was substantially filled out substantially enough to hold periodic inspections by January of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, do you know how many members they had, the Patriotic League, I mean, in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said you read the book by Mr. Sefer Halilovic, A Smart Strategy?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that he was the commander of the headquarters of the chief of staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1990?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe 1992, was that your statement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, the Defence has a copy of one part of that book by Mr. Sefer Halilovic. On page 120, he talks about how many members the Patriotic League had with reference to 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pilipovic, are you going to tender this page or what is your intention? As you know, you should indicate when providing a document to the witness whether you want to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Defence would like for this page to be tendered as proof on behalf of the Defence. I believe I marked with the number of 104, unless I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your numbering, Ms. Pilipovic, all the other documents you have shown to the witness were already part of the document that is tendered by the Prosecution, that is the report of Mr. Donia, and the footnote to it. So, Madam Registrar thinks we are D100 and not D104, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mrs. Kelly tried to explain it to me so it is a relief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You are doing your utmost.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, on page 120, you will see that there is an English version as well, Mr. Sefer Halilovic talks about the spring of 1992 and in para 2 says, "But I must say that at military talks in the village of Mehurici near Travnik when we marked the anniversary, and the current organisers have not invited me, even though I am one of the organisers... They established what -- the Patriotic League had at that time between 60 to 70.000 [Real-time transcript read in error: 60 to 7000"] armed members and that number increased day by day because military organisation was formed."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, would you agree that the figures referred to by Mr. Sefer Halilovic here as to the number of members of the patriotic league are acceptable?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. I think the meeting in Mehurici was, if I am not mistaken, in March. So this would be a number in a sense on the probably March, early April period. I think early you had asked me about 1991, and I would think that this number would be way too high for 1991 but would be maybe a little high, but about right for this period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In order to avoid whatever misunderstanding, for the transcript, page 53, line 13, should read 60 to 70.000 armed members and not to 60 to 7000 armed members.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now in the transcript, on the new line on page 54, line 1, the number has even reduced to 60 to 70, but it is 60 to 70.000 armed members. It is a total confusion at this moment because where I said what it was not, it surprisingly gives the number it should be. So for the last and final time, page 53, line 13, should be 60 to 70.000 armed members. Yes, that is correct. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, you told us yesterday that the BH army was set up on the 15th of April, 1992 starting on the basis of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I told you yesterday or testified yesterday that the unified command of the Territorial Defence forces was established on 15 April, 1992 and that organisation subsequently became the army of BH.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about the members of the Patriotic League and the members of the Green Berets joining the armed forces of BH?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, my knowledge is more of the Patriotic League and the -- a couple of the commanders of the Patriotic League have written that the organisation came under the command of the unified TO staff on the 15th of April, 1992. I am sorry, I don't know the status of the Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, in your report, you claim that the SDS regionalisation made it possible for itself to establish control over the Territorial Defence. Have I phrased this question correctly? That, when carrying out regionalisation, it established control over the Territorial Defence; is that what you claimed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I put it a little bit differently. The Territorial Defence units in each municipality came under the political authorities in most situations from -- in those municipalities, which meant that in municipalities with a Serbian majority and SDS control of the municipality Assemblies, those TO organisations, in most instances, came under the SDS control. In municipalities where the Bosnian Muslims had a majority or where there was a mixed situation, in most of those situations, the TO units came under the Republican TO authorities, and, subsequently, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Certainly regionalisation assisted in some municipalities in that SDS control over a TO unit, but probably only in a few municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether in the territory of the city of Sarajevo in which areas did the SDS establish control over the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure about each and everything municipality, but certainly Ilidza, Pale, Ilijas -- beyond that, I am not certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us when, and at what time, the SDS established control?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think probably was different for each municipality. Pale certainly was very early. But I can't give you specific dates, so the answer is really, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us which brigade of the Territorial Defence of the regional staff in Sarajevo was controlled by the SDS?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the division of the Territorial Defence took place in municipalities but also at the republican level and that this happened after the division in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, do you know whether in June 1991 Alija Izetbegovic, that is to say the leadership of the SDA and those in power in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, so we are talking about June 1991, do you know whether they made it impossible for the JNA to be filled up with recruits in reservists who were born in Bosnia-Herzegovina and at that time, the JNA was a legitimate institution still?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are claiming that no such decision was adopted?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked me whether the SDA leadership made it impossible for the JNA to be filled up with recruits and reservists and the answer to that is, no, they did not make it impossible.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say, "they did not prevent this, they did not make it impossible," are you telling us that reservists and recruits from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so people who were born in the territory of the Bosnia-Herzegovina, went to the JNA? And I am referring to Muslims right now.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to clarify something. I would just like to clarify this issue now. Is it correct to say that from June 1991, the reservists from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina who were of Muslim nationality did not respond to the call-up papers from the JNA? Would it be correct to claim that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it would not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Donia, in your report you claim that the Yugoslav People's Army became an instrument of the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I made that statement appropriate to any period prior to May 12th, 1992. Do you have a citation where I state that?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, I shall try to find that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can I assist you, Ms. Pilipovic. Are you referring to page 8 in the English language where it reads: "In the first five months of 1992, the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina was gradually transformed from a Yugoslav force composed of various nationalities into an instrument of SDS policies operating in the name of Serbian national interests." Is that the part that you are referring to? Could you please then answer the question, Mr. Donia.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would, I think, stand by this formulation. A gradual transformation that culminated in the event of May -- or the decision of May 12th, 1992 to actually make the JNA units in Bosnia-Herzegovina, remake them into the Bosnian Serb army. The events of April and early May, 1992 contributed substantially to that process, but it still -- there is considerable evidence of an independent JNA policy, independent of the SDS as late as the first several days of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, on the basis of which documents did you arrive at such a conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, the deliberations of the Serbian -- Assemblies of the Serbian people, in particular, the addresses of Dr. Karadzic, who back in late 1991 indicated that the JNA was not really at the disposal of the SDS and couldn't be counted upon by the SDS to carry out its policies. By March of 1992, in some of the minutes we have been looking at, he makes a statement - in fact, there are a couple of statements - that the army is no problem and can be counted on, in effect, to support SDS aims. That doesn't mean it was subordinated to the SDS - I think there is an important difference - but rather that the command element of the JNA was working in tandem with the SDS to achieve certain limited aims.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, could you provide us with the name of one JNA commander who was appointed as commander by the SDS? That is to say, was appointed as a commander of the army and of the corps.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you see in the statement that I have excerpted from the 1995 minutes of the Serbian Assembly, Radovan Karadzic claimed that his nominee, Radic, had been made commander of the second military district, upon his, that is Karadzic's, nomination. On the other hand, it is clear that that designation, the appointment, was not Karadzic's to make and such appointments were not made by the SDS at that time or, for that matter, later in the formal sense; those were not party appointments.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, could you mention a plan or an action by the JNA which was planned by the leadership of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think I have made clear that that would not be something that would have taken place in this period. There probably were some decisions to distribute arms to SDS members or local Serbs that would have been initiated by the SDS and the result of efforts to persuade JNA officers to so distribute arms. But I think that would be the extent of the actual SDS ability to influence JNA decisions. At this point we are talking about prior to May 12th.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, do you know when the JNA left Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Parts of it left -- concerns fortification in May of 1992. I think parts probably left in late April, but most of the weaponry and a large number of the personnel never left, didn't leave in this time period anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of a document being signed, according to which the JNA was going to withdraw on the 4th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, would you agree that up until the signature on the 4th of May, up until it signed that document on the 4th of May, 1992, would you agree that the JNA was a legitimate military force in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, regardless of the fact that on the 6th of April, the European Community recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us why not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA was asked to depart Bosnia-Herzegovina by the leadership of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was then an independent state. So it would at least call into question whether that was a legitimate military force on the territory of a sovereign state at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, we are close to the time where we usually have a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I also ask you how much time you would still need approximately? If we have a break to close to 6.00, how much time would you still need do you think? We are coming to the weekend and you know that I always become a bit nervous towards the weekend how far we have come that week.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that I will have finished my cross-examination by the end of this hearing, and perhaps even earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, do you have any idea of how much time you would need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this stage, very little time indeed, a matter of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A matter of minutes. And during the break, I will try to find out what questions from the Bench are still to be expected. We will have a break until 5 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 5.57 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we had a spare set of the tabbed binders so we have given that spare set to the accused. Thank you. THE COURT: Yes. That's good, so that he is better able to follow what happens. Ms. Pilipovic, I just inform you that the Chamber has a few questions, but not many. That means a couple of minutes for Mr. Ierace, not many questions from the Chamber, so if we would -- if we could conclude this Friday, that would be fine. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, on page 10 of your report you mentioned the demonstrations in front of the Assembly building on the 6th of April. You wrote that six demonstrators lost their lives and the others scattered about and ran way. It is just before the footnote 69, page 10 of the translation; I do apologise, Mr. Donia. You wrote that the BH police, when they got to the site, realised that people who opened fire left the city together with the key leaders of SDS. Footnote 69?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, did you mean to say that the people who left the city together with the key leaders were the people who opened fire on the citizens? Because you said that the police found that the people who opened fire left the hotel.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's most of them had left the hotel, and I think that the reports are that a small number of them were arrested.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your stay in Sarajevo, did you find out who actually shot at the citizens gathering in front of the building?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The names of those persons, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, you told us that you follow the press in Sarajevo. You even referred to Slobodna Bosna magazine; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave two citations to Slobodna Bosna in the course of the paper. I would say that following the press in Sarajevo was probably a hopeless task. I try to follow it in the main, but it is certainly not the case that I see everything that comes out.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your stay in Sarajevo, whilst working on the history of that period, did you find out and did you obtain any information as to Juka Prazina might be? Have you ever heard that name?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, have you in the course of your stay in Sarajevo, more specifically in 2000, did you read an article in Slobodna Bosna written by Mrs. Medina Mladic, and she said, "Juka Prazina told us that our snipers were shooting at the people in front of the Assembly building"? Have you ever seen such an article?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we do have a copy of that article so we can present the witness with the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if he, of course -- perhaps he first answers the question as to whether he has ever seen it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have not seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the next question is what you could ask the witness about something he has not seen before, but perhaps I will leave it for a while. Ms. Pilipovic, you understand what the concern of the Chamber is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, do you have any knowledge of and did you ever, in the course of your stay and work in Sarajevo, find out that the people in front of the Assembly building, the citizens gathered there, were shot at by the snipers from the terrorist group under the command of Juka Prazina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And if I tell you that the Slobodna Bosna magazine published such an article, can you accept that this might be true?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to the question. It has no probative value, given the answers by the witness to the last question and similar questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Pilipovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my questions and the submitting of this article were addressed to Mr. Donia for the simple reason that, in his statement, Mr. Donia mentioned that fire was opened in front of the Holiday Inn and that the demonstrators were shot at and that the people responsible were the ones who were together with the leaders of the SDS party, during this stay in Sarajevo and his work in that area of his research in that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially since Mr. Donia seems to be referring to literature and newspaper articles published in Sarajevo. Amongst other sources, he also mentioned the Slobodna Bosna magazine. I thought that for the sake of check the credibility of Mr. Donia, I would present him with a document that he must have come across as a historian, he must have had the opportunity to read it. However, if Mr. Donia doesn't recognise it, no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, you are mixing up a lot of things. On the other hand, even if you have not seen the newspaper article, if this is just an assumption, if you would know who was responsible, then you could tell that if this newspaper says that someone else is responsible could not be true. But I do not know whether this is the knowledge of Mr. Donia, so -- but I couldn't say that the question has no probative value at all, so therefore the objection is denied. But perhaps you ask the question in such a way that we don't get theoretical answers, but practical answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, do you have any knowledge of the fact that it was the Juka Prazina group that was shooting at the citizens in front of the Assembly building?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me point out that this article refers to 5 April, 1992. My statement in the paper refers to 6 April, 1992. As you know, there were demonstrations on both days and both came under fire. The first day's demonstration was dispersed with not a lot of blood spilt. I don't think there was actually any injuries. The 6th was a much more serious attack. So I would respectfully note that the document that you have given me has no relevance to the statement that I made in the paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, you said that the day when Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised was the 6th of April and that was when there was a lot of shooting in Sarajevo. Do you know anything about whether, on the 5th of April, there were any demonstrations in front of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about there being any shots fired at the demonstrators in front of the building on the 5th of April?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 5th of April, snipers from the sniper terrorist group under the command of Juka Prazina were the ones shooting at the citizens in front of the building?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who did that shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Donia. In your report you refer to the 2nd of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on that day, the Muslim army, about 500 armed individuals, attacked the centre of the JNA in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's quite correct statement. The JNA command -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. well, ask me more. I don't think that statement is correct, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about one lieutenant and one soldier having been wounded on that day in front of the JNA community centre?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you -- I mean, you are referring to the events of the 3rd of May, 1992. Do you know anything about the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina attacking a group of soldiers on that day and they were headed by Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's two questions there. On the 3rd of May, there was an attack by Territorial Defence forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina on a convoy that was moving through the streets of Sarajevo. Alija Izetbegovic was in one of the armoured personnel carriers because he had been taken hostage by the JNA the previous day when he returned to the airport from international negotiations. So, I would say I don't think they were headed by Alija Izetbegovic at that point, since he was actually in one of the armoured personnel carriers of the convoy that was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, in your report on page 11 of the B/C/S version, after the reply that the Territorial Defence did attack the -- well, could you explain what you meant by the failed offensive [Realtime transcript read in error "defensive"] of the JNA on the 2nd and the 3rd of May? On page 11.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's see. I'm not --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Just before strategic goals.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 2nd of May, the JNA brought armoured vehicles across the river and toward the Presidency building from several directions. This battle is recounted in the several memoir accounts and also in the press reporting at the time and the commission of experts report. Those armoured vehicle reached the park directly in front of the city government building where they were stopped by anti-armour weapons in the possession of the Territorial Defence forces and several of those armoured personnel carriers burned until late in the day on that square. That offensive, apparently directed at taking the Presidency building, failed and at the same time, roughly the same time, Izetbegovic was detained at the Sarajevo airport. So by the end of the 2nd of May, there was a situation where the JNA command element, which was in the headquarters component in Bistrik wanted to exit the city and, of course, the Bosnians wanted their presidency -- president back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for the sake of the record, page 66, line 11, should read "offensive," instead of "defensive."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, you claim that the leaders of SDS formulated their strategic goals by the beginning of May, 1992. I am referring to the minutes of the Assembly meeting of the 12th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe my statement was that they formulated their strategic goals in the course of two meetings, one at Graz on the 6th of May and one at Banja Luka on the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, we are talking about five or six strategic goals defined by the Assembly of the Republika Srpska on the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or six.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Do you make a distinction between the Assembly and the SDS as a party?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Formally there was a distinction. In practical reality, the Assembly was consisted of almost exclusively of SDS members. So I think in the day-to-day reality, there really was not much difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So the Assembly as such, as an constitution is being compared to the SDS as a party by you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I would say there was virtually complete overlap between the two. There were a few members of the Assembly who were not SDS members and there were certainly some SDS members whose did not share in the views and conclusions of the Assembly. But the overlap was very substantial. But I concur that these are two different institutions. Formally, they are two different organisations.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Donia. Do you consider it as not legitimate that after the start of the hostilities, the Parliament starts defining the goals of the war? In other words, defining the goals of the war, is it within the area of competence of Parliament?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have an opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that the strategic goals as defined by the Assembly on the 12th of May, 1992, for the most part are goals which were accepted at Dayton except the one pertaining to having a part of the coast, that strategic goal?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So we cannot agree that those were the legitimate goals and that they were legitimately chosen and formulated as such?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know if they were legitimate or not. They were -- they were chosen, they were formulated, and what their level of legitimacy was in the constitutional sense, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Donia, can you agree with me that the most authentic minutes are the ones which are the shorthand minutes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in your opinion, whenever we are talking about any meeting at all, what is the most authentic document reflecting whatever has been said at a meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are minutes and there is a transcript. And in this instance, for example, one deals with transcript derived from a tape-recording made of the session. That should be the most accurate and complete record of the deliberations and conclusion of the Assembly. It is far superior to the shorthand minutes that were taken at many such sessions throughout Bosnia during this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are telling us that the most accurate source of information would be a transcript or a tape-recording?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly superior to the shorthand minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: But we can also agree that the shorthand minutes have -- arrive at a certain level of accuracy?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Often that is the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Donia, in your report, footnote number 83, you refer to the minutes on the 12th or, rather, on the 14th of May 1992. I think it is the last minutes. It is in the binder 2-2, the last pages of the minutes in the second binder.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, was it a short -- are these shorthand minutes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us on what basis you made this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is a set of minutes that are typical of shorthand notations made at minutes in this period, often with incomplete sentences and one or two sentences -- sentence summaries of statements that clearly were longer by some of the speakers. I believe we have a signature page at the end of the B/C/S. Probably more than anything else, the absence of the more precise quotations or word-for-word quotations would indicate that these are shorthand rather than -- shorthand minutes, rather than transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you agree with me that these minutes are simply an interpretation of what certain of the speakers present at the meeting said, especially if you look at page two of these minutes, and page three as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the person in this role is tasked with summarising speeches by the individual person. So I characterise them as summaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, would you say that this -- these minutes were taken by someone, that this record was made after the meeting was held? Do you think that this record was made after the meeting, someone who was present and who compiled the record and interpreted what was happening at the meeting and, let's say, typed it on a typewriter? Would you admit that this was possible?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the normal procedure in such a situation was for a person to take shorthand notes and then to type them up on a typewriter at some point, reasonably short in time after the conclusion of the meeting. Typically the same day, but not always.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So we agree that these minutes could have been compiled by someone who signed this minutes and it could have been compiled after the meeting was held, but that it was compiled on that same day?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is safe to conclude that they were typed after the meeting, but probably initially compiled in the course of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, in your report you pointed out that that meeting was presided over by Mr. Stanislav Galic. If we have a better look at the minutes, that is to say, that the first page of the minutes, the first page of the minutes where it says, after number 11, "The President of the autonomous region of Kljuc told those present of the objectives of the meeting and allowed Mr. Colonel Galic to speak. On the basis of what the President said of the autonomous region of Kljuc agreed to those who were present would be possible to draw the conclusion that the President presided over the meeting that was held on that day."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not able to put my finger on exactly where I expressed that in the report, but it was clear to me that the person presiding over the meeting was not General Galic, but the president of the -- of Kljuc, who -- of the Serbian Assembly of Kljuc, who then turned over the meeting to him to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Donia. So according to your interpretation on page 12 in the B/C/S, which starts with paragraph 4, "The appointment of General Mladic, the transfer of the Yugoslav people's army into the army of Republika -- will enable the civil organs -- " THE COURT: Mr. Donia, did you find it? It is in the English version, page 11, the second last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I would -- that is simply not -- my formulation there is in error. It is very much the case that he was not presiding over the meeting, but he did address it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, thank you. So you agree that Colonel Galic was a guest, since he was in command of the unit whose zone of responsibility included the municipalities we have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a guest and a participant.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Donia, we have had the opportunity of becoming familiar with the decision of the Assembly, the decision of the 12th of May, 1992, and also to take cognisance of the strategic objectives. The strategic objective we are interested at the moment is the strategic objective number 5, which states that the objective of dividing Sarajevo into a Serbian and Muslim part, that this is the objective; would you agree that in the formulation of this 5th objective, which is to divide Sarajevo in to a Serbian and Muslim part?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the formulation at the meeting of the 12th of May, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In your report on page 12, you told us that at that meeting, Mr. Milan Malidza repeated the six strategic objectives which have been accepted two days earlier on in Banja Luka. However, his formulation of the 5th priority of Sarajevo was more correct than the version that had been officially made known. It was said that Sarajevo had to be either divided or levelled with the ground.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We may be encountering a problem of translation somewhere, but my original report was that -- stated that this formulation was more specific than the officially published version.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Donia. You would agree that Mr. Milan Malidza incorrectly interpreted this. He didn't repeat all the six strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he incorrectly interpreted it or not. He stated it differently and may have stated his understanding of it. No one stood up at the meeting and corrected him, according to the minutes, so I don't know the nature of his reformulation of that objective other than to say, it certainly was more specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that it was possible for that to be his interpretation as a deputy. He was present there, was present in the Assembly and I would especially like to underline that the strategic objectives, all six of them and, especially the 5th objective, does not include such a formulation.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it can be characterised as his interpretation of the six points.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, you said on that same page, it begins with "Colonel Galic proposed, that the six strategic objectives be adopted." Would you agree with me that your interpretation is not correct, your interpretation that Colonel Galic proposed that the six strategic objectives be adopted?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, in the record, the last page of the minutes on page 4, it says, "At the end of the meeting Colonel Galic suggested the following proposal -- the following conclusions, to have the conclusions implemented, the conclusions from the meeting in Banja Luka," so the word "adopting" -- the word "adopt" cannot be identify with the word "implement". They are not the same words. In the first part of his conclusion, he says the conclusions from the Banja Luka meeting should be implemented but they should also be forwarded to the command of the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that -- I agree, at least in the English, this is the statement and I am assuming that one of those decisions at the meeting was the adoption of the six strategic objectives.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, would you agree with me that to implement something and to adopt something, these are two different concepts.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me the term "implement" is stronger than "adopt" and would encompass the adoption of it. They are two different words, to be sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that General Galic suggested that these minutes, that is to they, conclusions should be forwarded to the commands of units and municipalities, so that he was not aware of the actual contents of the minutes, that is to say, the conclusion of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That question is not -- I don't think is answerable from the document. I am sure he knows, but I don't know that from this statement one could conclude whether he was or was not familiar with the specific decisions of the meeting in Banja Luka. You know, he proposed the, what, seven conclusions that were adopted unanimously by the meeting, and one of those was to clearly implement the decision in Banja Luka. I think, in that sense, the document perhaps best speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that the following conclusion was that the current positions should be held and that they should be held without a conflict. It's the second item?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, defend them without war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, on page 13 on the same document, the interpretation of the statement -- you gave an interpretation of the statement of Mr. Malidza and under the strategic objective number 5 that Sarajevo should be either divided or razed with the ground, you came to the conclusion that this was closer to the intentions of many leaders of the SDS and military offices than the more moderate version that was adopted on the 12th of May and which is -- and which only mentions the division of the city. Is this your personal interpretation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my assessment of the various speeches made by a number of SDS leaders at the meeting of May 12th.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, if we carefully read the minutes of the 12th of May, and carry out an analysis of everything that was said by the deputies, would you agree with me, and I carried out a careful analysis, that none of the deputies said that Sarajevo should be razed to the ground. There were various formulations but nothing of that kind was said at that meeting, that is quite true?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are many different variations of the way Sarajevo should be destroyed at that meeting, but I do not find the one that said "Sarajevo should be razed to the ground."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, would you agree that up until the time General Galic came to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, came to its head, the political and military -- the political, military and territorial division of Sarajevo had been concluded, and I would like to say that he became the command of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps on the 6th of December, [as interpreted] 1992?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would -- yes, I concur but would say that the lines of confrontation were not completely stable from that point on. There were shifts and changes in lines of confrontation after September of 1992. But I think that -- or I think that the date is September of 1992. I see September 1992 -- I see December in the transcript, but I would agree that the division was complete.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has concluded its cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Pilipovic. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps my learned colleague could clarify that she did mean the 6th of September, 1992. I refer to page 75, line 20 of the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is what I said, but I don't know why it says December in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, you just have been asked some questions about page 11 of the English version of your report. Might I clarify whether you said in effect during that questioning that you wanted to change something at the bottom of page 11. Did you intend that or not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think the question was pertained to the -- my statement that on 14 May, 1992, the commander of the 30th Partisan Division, Colonel Stanislav Galic, presided over a meeting. And yes, I would change that to say "participated" in a meeting. It is certainly true that he proposed, according to the minutes, all of the conclusions of the meeting, but formally did not preside in the sense that he did not open the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Does it appear from the minutes that at the outset of the meeting, the president set out the goals of the meeting as he saw them, apparently referred to the present guests, and then it seems straight after that gave the floor to Colonel Galic?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Therefore he was the first speaker of substance, so it seems, and he was the last speaker of substance?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Going to the last page of those minutes, it was pointed out that one of the proposals made by Colonel Galic to be adopted by the meeting was that present positions be held and defended without war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thereafter the other proposed measures for adoption included the proposal of the continued growth of the army; is that so?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The obtaining of further weapons and equipment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And the maintenance of the economy on a wartime footing?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As well as the commendation of soldiers for their combat results achieved so far?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to this issue of whether there was some misunderstanding about goal five, do the minutes record that the president presented the conclusions to the meeting of the earlier meeting at Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And does it appear thereafter the reference to Sarajevo being either divided or razed to the ground?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I would like to ask you some other questions about your report while it is in front of you. Earlier, in our session yesterday, you were asked a question by Mr. Piletta-Zanin about the nature of some academic work undertaken by you, in particular, having regard to your curriculum vitae, the nature of a dissertation you undertook in 1976 for your doctorate. And I think you said yesterday that, "The topic of my doctorate thesis was the political and social life of the Muslims of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1878 until 1908." Would you please look at page 31 of your report, that being the last page of your curriculum vitae?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You have told us yesterday what the topic was. Having regard to the precise title, is there firstly a misprint, in that "1978" should be "1878"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is a title and work I would like to forget, actually. But I clearly have not rendered it correctly here.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And I take it that "1914" should be "1908."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, 1914 is correct. The work was principally prior to 1908 but it did continue to 1914.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Staying with your report, you were asked some questions about an incident in, I think it was May 1992, where some members of a wedding party involving individuals from the Serbian community were attacked, and that was in the context of the start of conflict. That is the context of the questions in cross-examination. That appears at the bottom of page 8 of the English version of your report.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in March.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, March. Having regard to the content of your footnote 63, have you come across some references to the perpetrator being responsible for some earlier offences, including murder and rape, and that individual having received psychiatric attention in the past?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You were asked some questions today in relation to some instructions issued in December of 1991 entitled: "Instructions for the organisation and activity of organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina in extraordinary circumstances." That appears at tab 26 to 31. Do you have that volume in front of you? The spine should indicate volume 2- 2.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You were asked some questions about that document. One of those questions appears in the English version of LiveNote at page 40, line 9. You were referred to this report and then asked, "Is it logical if in one municipality one of the parties got the majority, was it logical for them to organise power there?" I think it is fair to say that the suggestion was that the majority ethnic group was surely entitled to organise power in a municipality if they held the majority. Do you remember being asked that question?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And you referred to the legitimate government institutions being already well in place. Did you have in mind the government institutions of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The government institutions of Bosnia-Herzegovina and of each of the 109 municipalities which were part of the governmental structure of the socialist republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As of December 1991, what was the nature of the representative organ of the government, in other words, was it a Parliament or an Assembly or something else?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina was the representative body that was the legislative organ of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Were the members of that Assembly elected or appointed?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All were elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was the profile of the Assembly in relation to its ethnic composition singular or was there multiple representation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were representatives from all three major nationalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Having regard to the question and the suggestion in it that the majority group was entitled to engage in, indeed, to organise for itself power, would you now look at the document in front of you, in particular, having regard to the number in the top right-hand corner, page 2624. Do you have that in front of you? That is the title page of the instructions.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The top left-hand corner is identified as a document of a party, that is a political party?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Being the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is it also described as being strictly confidential?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Does the document bear instructions for two types of municipalities, firstly, those where the Serb people form a majority, being Variant A; and secondly, those where the Serbian people are in a minority, being Variant B?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do the instructions require the establishment of assemblies in each of the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The establishment of a Serbian Assembly in each municipality, both Variant A and Variant B.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Indeed, in requiring the establishment of a Serbian Assembly, do Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the instructions specifically require that the only member of the assemblies are to be Serbian?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do the instructions also require for the taking of control of the various organs of government?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel for the Prosecution please slow down a little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, I do understand that you trying to keep your promise that it would take a couple of minutes, but nevertheless the interpreters have to interpret.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do the instructions require that all of those organs are to be controlled by either Serbs or persons who have expressed allegiance or support of the aims of the party?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi has one or two questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Witness, I would like you to explain to me, if you could, a few details, a few minor details. On page 11 of your report, of your testimony, you quoted the date, you mentioned the date 14th of May, it was, and you spoke about -- and if we then turn to the bottom of the page 83, it says, and I am reading it in English -- is that the same Colonel Galic.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But he was the commander of the 30th division or was he the commander of the 1st Partisan Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I think that in the Serbian version I can see that it says the 30th part division, the 12th of May, so there is after all -- this meeting took place on the 14th or the 12th?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding, in looking at the document at the time, was that it took place on the 14th. But I see Your Honour's point that this is -- the date, that the 12th occurs in my citation of the B/C/S original and I am -- would have to go to the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move to -- move on to another issue. I am quoting you. You are still speaking about Colonel Galic [In English] "Without further fighting." [Interpretation] And then he suggested a meeting every 15 days with the presidents of civilian municipalities. Did that actually take place? Did they meet? What was the position of General Galic at these meetings as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have not encountered any evidence of further meetings of this group together with General Galic. It appeared to me from the minutes that he was turning over to the presidents of the Serbian Assemblies the initiative for convening such meetings, but beyond that, I have no indication or run across any documentation of such further meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it is possible that there were other meetings?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, sir. If I ask you one last question with regard to your conclusion. You stated -- you made two claims. You said that there was shelling, and I quote you in English, [In English] "Advantage to shell the city periodically to damage and destroy..." [Interpretation] So you suggested or you advanced the material fact, that is to say the shelling, and you nevertheless assumed that there was an intention which accompanied it and that was the intention, the intention was to damage cultural monuments and religious monuments, and then you say [In English] Electricity..." End of quote. [Interpretation] This intention, did you come to the conclusion that there was such an intention with regard to -- on the basis of the report from the special emissary of the United Nations or was this on the basis of the personal research you carried out, or is it an observation, the subject of your own reflection? I would like to know what your opinion is.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say, principally, the reports of observers on the scene and the pattern of the destruction in -- now, please note that I am speaking of the period before September, 1992, but the destruction of certain cultural monuments, particularly the -- I could name them, but there were several -- appeared to be quite calculated and deliberate in terms of the types of shells that were directed at them and the consistency of the attacks on particular targets. And that observation is shared by the United Nations observers in at least one case, the case of the library. And so I would just perhaps return to the statement that the overwhelming military advantage both permitted this, and in a sense, facilitated this kind of very specific targeting of cultural monuments, particularly cultural monuments that attested to the city's multi-ethnic life. More so than religious institutions, for example, of any particular group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Donia, before I could even put a question to you, I first have to ask the interpreters. I have four relatively short questions to Mr. Donia. Could we conclude today, or otherwise we would have to invite Mr. Donia to come back, Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If it assists you, Mr. President, in your decision, Mr. Donia has to come back any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I know that he is almost a full resident these times. But, of course, just for a couple of minutes, would the booth agree or strongly object against four more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am listening to the wrong channel. Thank you very much for your kind cooperation, especially for a Friday, late in the afternoon. Mr. Donia, a couple of questions have been put to you in relation to a -- well, whether or not Muslim reservists or recruits would not respond to being called to the JNA. Do you know anything about it? The questions did not give many information -- the answers to the question didn't give many information, but do you know anything about it and what do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The SDA came to the conclusion in the summer of 1991 that it was not going to support these mobilisations, which were quite frequent and occurred at the level of various units. And in many individual mobilisations, such as the one in the Bosnian Krajina in late June 1991, the SDA leaders informally urged Muslim recruits not to join, but many of them did in any case. The same situation prevailed in a mobilisation of troops in Prijedor in September 1991, where the local SDS organisation understood that the Sarajevo party was not opposed to the mobilisations, and so essentially took no position. And large numbers of Muslims participated in that mobilisation and, in fact, the first casualty within that unit in Croatia was a Muslim. So, for some time, the SDA general position in opposition to such mobilisations had only modest effect on Muslim participation. However, in -- I think it is September 29, 1991 -- they specifically requested local units to ignore the mobilisations. In other words, they authorised them to stand aside from the process. They never specifically prevented or obstructed the participation in those mobilisations until after the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so I do understand that although you couldn't agree with Ms. Pilipovic, that there was some factual basis in those questions.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next question about the 15th of October meeting, it is not quite clear to me. It reads: "After the Assembly had been adjourned for the day by its President and the Bosnian Serb delegates had departed, HDZ and SDA delegates reconvened the session and passed the declaration of sovereignty." It doesn't say anything about the way it was reconvened. Were the -- after the Assembly had been adjourned, were the Bosnian Serb delegates informed about -- leave apart whether this could be done by the HDZ and SDA delegates -- but were they informed about the reconvention of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apparently, they were not informed, no. It was a trick by the HDZ and SDA delegates to reconvene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is clear. Then I -- have you explained to us, in relation to, as far as I can see, the handwritten part even on the B/C/S version on the meeting of the 14th of May that you said, well, the meeting decided to implement the strategic goals or measures and therefore they adopted them. Now, it might be a matter of language, but my first question is: Do you find any specific reference to adopting the earlier, two days earlier adopted, strategic goals by this meeting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only that they were listed by Mr. Mladic at the same meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It reads that it was presented?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were presented, and so I agree this is a matter of language, and perhaps the formulation that's in the minutes is the best one to accept. I find no further evidence than what you have in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You also explain that implementing is even stronger adopting. That was part of your testimony. And there we might come in the field of language. It is my understanding, but please correct me if I am wrong, that implementing a goal or a strategy could be done by a subordinate - I am not talking about whether it's an army or a university body or governmental body - could be implemented even if you would not personally adopt the measures, but since you are under a duty to do so or -- so I have some difficulty in understanding why implementing is even stronger than adopting. But perhaps you could explain what you specifically meant when you testified. Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would certainly not argue the point with you at all. To me implementation suggests an immediate action to take steps to advance a particular agenda or set of goals. Now, I think I would just, in general, fall back on the context of the document and point out that it is clear that everyone is in agreement about the basic steps to be taken, moving forward here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that also implicate in your opinion that -- I mean, if you know how to implement a certain measure, does that automatically mean that you would have taken that measure by yourself as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT DONIA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think it does not. I would agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, we have no difficulty any more as far as the language is concerned. These were my questions. Mr. Donia, it's late. It's Friday evening. You have answered, well, not too many questions of the party who called you, but that is because of the specific procedure under Rule 94 bis. So you had to answer a lot of questions in cross-examination by Ms. Pilipovic. You answered the questions of the Bench. I would like to thank you very much for coming and giving those answers to this Chamber. It needs answers to questions in order to perform its task. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's an honour, Mr. President

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will then adjourn until next Monday morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 7.15, p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 22nd day of April, 2002, at 9.00 a.m.
